content.title: Rebuttal for reviewer XMRc
content.comment:
# Rebuttal for reviewer XMRc
## 1. The channel-wise normalization [a] and k-nearest neighbor clustering [b] are proposed many years ago. Both of them are widely used in the computer vision field. Therefore, the novelty of the paper is limited.
### **Response**: 
The major contribution of this work lies in identifying and analyzing for the first time a fundamental problem of feature acquisition bias in deep learning, and a novel and robust feature acquisition network (RFANet) is proposed to address this intrinsic weakness of current FSFGIC models.

Normalization and k-nearest neighbor are common components in metric-learning based image classification methods such as in DN4, CovaMNet, BSNet, and ATL-Net. These two components are not contributions of this work.

[a] Wu, Zuxuan, et al. "Dcan: Dual channel-wise alignment networks for unsupervised scene adaptation." Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV). 2018.

[b] Boiman, Oren, Eli Shechtman, and Michal Irani. "In defense of nearest-neighbor based image classification." 2008 IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. IEEE, 2008.

## 2. The authors should provide evidence to support the claim that DA operations increase the quantization noise of images.
### **Response**: 
When performing data augmentation on digital images, the new image is slightly different from the original image as a digital image is represented by values quantized to integers at locations quantized to image grids. Such quantization noise often causes image blur and loss of information.

## 3. The authors should compare with more latest works in the experiment, such as [c][d]. [c] PaCL: Part-level Contrastive Learning for Fine-grained Few-shot Image Classification, ACM MM 2022. In fact, [d] achieves better performance than the proposed approach in the CUB dataset.
### **Response**: 
Our paper was submitted to ICLR2023 (Sept 28, 2022) before [c] was published on October 10, 2022.

FRN [d] is a state-of-the-art method, which is used as one of the benchmarks in this paper (see Table 8). In our paper, the standard “Categories Sampler” experimental setting is used in the same way as used by the other 8 benchmarks (see Table 8), such as DN4, BSNet, and AT-Net. The results reported in paper [d] is obtained in a different experimental setting not comparable to any other 8 benchmarks and our method, thus cannot be directly used for performance comparison. The FRN [d] results in Table 8 are obtained by us, using the code provided by the authors of [d] under the standard “Categories Sampler” experimental setting. Our obtained results of FRN method on the CUB dataset for the 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot FSFGIC tasks are 78.07 and 89.33 respectively, which are the same results of the FRN method as reported in the article [e]. In summary, the performance of our method is significantly better than [d] on the CUB dataset as shown in Table 8.

[c] Wang, Chuanming, Huiyuan Fu, and Huadong Ma. "PaCL: Part-level Contrastive Learning for Fine-grained Few-shot Image Classification." Proceedings of the 30th ACM International Conference on Multimedia. 2022.

[d] Wertheimer, Davis, Luming Tang, and Bharath Hariharan. "Few-shot classification with feature map reconstruction networks." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2021.

[e] Yangfan Li and Chunjiang Bian. Few-shot fine-grained ship classification with a foreground-aware feature map reconstruction network. IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing, 60:1–12, 2022

## 4. The ablation experiments should study why the normalization and geometric average operations contribute to performance improvement.
### **Response**: 
For our proposed geometric average measure, it has already been described in detail in the ablation studies of the article (Influence of n DA operations on the query image for FSFGI) as follows:
```
Based on the backbone of Conv64F, four different n (n belongs to {2,3,4,5}) are selected for performing 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot FSFGIC tasks on the Stanford Dogs and Standford Cars datasets with a fixed parameter k (k=1). The results on the 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot tasks are shown in Table 5. It is observed from Table 5 that when n equals 3, the proposed RFANet achieves the allover best classification performance. Therefore, DA operations on the query image with n=3 is recommended for our designed architecture.
```

Normalization operation is a widely used standard component in most metric-learning based methods such as DN4, CovaMNet, BSNet, and ATL-Net. It is not a contribution of this paper.

content.title: Rebuttal for reviewer wpgM
content.comment:
# Rebuttal for reviewer wpgM
## 1. Some words (e.g. “bias in features”, “quantization noise”) need more explanation at the time it was first presented.
### **Response**: 
- **Bias in features** denotes the deviation of features from different instances (such as augmented versions) of each input image.
- **Quantization noise**: Image mapping processes, such as applying DA operations, introduce errors because a digital image is quantized to image grids, which is named quantization noise in this paper.

These have been added in the revised version.

## 2. The language expression is a little repeated. There are some minor issues. e.g. In Table 4 the first column are wrongly written as the same.
### **Response**: These have been corrected. Thank you very much!

content.title: Rebuttal for reviewer jYXE
content.comment:
# Rebuttal to Reviewer jYXE
## 1. In the paper, authors present a PFANet for FSFG task to address the feature quantization bias, and three contributions are summarized. However, it is quite confusing about the specific definition of feature information, as well as the differences from contribution (1) and (3). The phrase "feature information" and "feature bias" are too general without the careful descriptions.

### **Response**:

- **Feature information** denotes the features obtained from different instances (such as augmented versions) of each input image.

- **Feature bias** denotes the deviation of features from different instances (such as augmented versions) of each input image.

These have been added in the revised version.

## 2. For the novelty part, seems authors propose to involve data augmentation to enhance the stability of the feature extraction, which is not novel in FSFG tasks.
### **Response**: This work identified and analyzed for the first time a fundamental problem, feature acquisition bias, in deep learning, and a novel and robust feature acquisition network (RFANet) is proposed to address this intrinsic problem in deep learning.

## 3. For experiments, 5-way experiments are conducted, what about 20-way (the case when class dictionary is large)?
### **Response**: As suggested, the 20-way 1-shot and 20-way 5-shot FSFGIC experiments on the Stanford Cars dataset have now been conducted and added into the article as follows:

```
The proposed RFANet has also been compared with DN4 on the Stanford Cars dataset for 20-way 1-shot and 20-way 5-shot FSFGIC tasks. 127 classes, 20 classes, and 49 classes of Stanford Cars dataset are randomly selected for training, validation, and testing respectively. Their classification accuracies are summarized in Table 7, consistently demonstrating the superior performance of the proposed method when class number increases.
```
Table 7: Comparison results on the Stanford Cars dataset based on Conv64F (20-way Accuracy (%) is evaluated.). 
| Model | Backbone | 1-shot | 5-shot |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| DN4 | Conv64F | 37.67$\pm$0.59 | 69.58$\pm$0.34 |
| RFANet | Conv64F | **48.55$\pm$0.48** | **77.65$\pm$0.31** |
## 4. If the performance gains are obtained by the data augmentation, ablation analysis should be conducted regarding which type of augmentation possess the most gain.

### **Response**:  The significant gains of classification accuracy obtained in this paper come from the RFANet’s capability in addressing the feature acquisition bias problem in current deep learning networks for FSFGIC tasks. 

As suggested, the proposed RFANet architecture with different DA has been conducted as follows:
```
Additional experiments are conducted for investigating the effect of different DA operations. Three different operations (i.e., random cropping, random horizontal flipping, and color jittering) are selected individually for performing 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot FSFGIC tasks respectively on the Stanford Cars dataset. Their results are shown in Table 6. It is observed that the proposed RFANet is more effective when applied on random cropping than on flipping and jittering.
```
Table 6: Comparison results on the Stanford Cars dataset based on Conv64F (5-way Accuracy (%) is evaluated.). 
| Model | 1-shot | 5-shot |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| RFANet (random cropping) | **68.19$\pm$0.67** | **89.38$\pm$0.36** |
| RFANet (random horizontal flipping) |  67.63$\pm$0.67 | 86.77$\pm$0.35 |
| RFANet (color jittering) |  64.60$\pm$0.66 | 87.59$\pm$0.39 |

content.title: Rebuttal for reviewer DzHP
content.comment:
# Rebuttal for Reviewer DzHP
## 1. The weakness is the ad-hoc definition of the features in Sec. 3.3.1. Although the authors present an ablation study, I am not convinced that Sec. 3.3.1 is more than a heuristic selection.
### **Response:** In this work, we identify and analyze for the first time a fundamental problem of existing metric-learning based FSFGIC methods which fail to effectively address the bias in feature acquisition from each input image that causes misclassification. The feature descriptors obtained by a convolutional embedding module from different DA operations on the same image have better consistency than those obtained from different images under different DA operations. To guide a convolution-based embedding model to obtain robust image feature information, the regularized feature descriptors of the augmented support image and the regularized feature descriptors of the n augmented query images are employed for similarity calculation for FSFGIC. This is still an open question and the proposed method is a first attempt on how to design a network that can effectively address the feature acquisition bias in deep learning.

## 2. I am also kind of puzzled that 1-NN performs best. I wonder whether there is a relation to Goering et al.: Nonparametric Part Transfer for Fine-grained Recognition, CVPR 2014. However, in the end, the performance justifies the approach.
### **Response:** In this work, 1-NN achieves the best classification performance on Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars datasets for both 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot FSFGIC tasks. We also found that 1-NN performs the best in the DN4 method [A] and NDPNet method [B]

[A]  Li, Wenbin, et al. "Revisiting local descriptor based image-to-class measure for few-shot learning." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2019.

[B] Zhang, Weichuan, et al. "NDPNet: A novel non-linear data projection network for few-shot fine-grained image classification." arXiv preprint arXiv:2106.06988 (2021).

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors report problems in data augmentation due to quantization noise. This introduces bias in the model, which is even more severe in fine-grained classification. They present a method that solves the dilemma between data augmentation and bias for a specific few-shot fine-grained classification model, namely c-way k-shot tasks. The idea is to augment each query image n-times and the support image only once. For all images, a feature embedding is generated by a CNN (for example, Resnet). Given a feature similarity based on the cosine distance, a k-NN selection is made that lead to an image-to-class similarity following a paper by Li (2019). The method is evaluated on five different fine-grained datasets. The performance is convincing compared to SotA methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strength of the paper is its simplicity in terms of use and the performance demonstrated in the experimental evaluation. Furthermore, as far as I can say, RFANet can be integrated into any episodic training mechanism, which is another plus for this work.

The weakness is the ad-hoc definition of the features in Sec. 3.3.1. Although the authors present an ablation study, I am not convinced that Sec. 3.3.1 is more than a heuristic selection. I am also kind of puzzled that 1-NN performs best. I wonder whether there is a relation to Goering et al.: Nonparametric Part Transfer for Fine-grained Recognition, CVPR 2014. However, in the end, the performance justifies the approach.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written and easy to follow. I like the experimental evaluation of 5 different tasks that support the authors' claim. However, only originality is moderate—especially the performance of 1-NN instead of the general case of k-NN puzzles me a bit. An explanation of this empirical result would have been an additional benefit of the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper convinces by the performance of an idea successfully implemented to FSFGIC. However, the concept itself is only moderately original and novel. There are no new theoretical concepts involved. The relation to the bias remains unclear to me. This term is misleading in the title. In addition, I would argue for better data augmentation to avoid quantization errors instead of such a new feature-generating network for end-to-end learning. 

After rebuttal and discussion with the other reviewers, I feel this paper has no strong theoretical contribution. On the other side, this lets me expect that the method and results can be easily reproduced, and the simplicity of a method can also be a strength. However, I would only see space for this paper if no other paper is available with a stronger methodological contribution.

Based on the overall feedback and revised manuscript, I'm willing to raise my score accordingly.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Existing fine-grained image classification methods use data augmentation operations to avoid overfitting. The authors claim that DA operation increases the quantization noise of images and leads to bias in the obtained feature. To overcome this, the authors propose to conduct channel-wise normalization and k-nearest neighbor clustering to capture more robust image features.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The idea of employing normalization operations to reduce the noise brought by data augmentation is simple and straightforward. The overall framework is clearly demonstrated in Figure2.
2. The proposed method is clearly explained in the paper. The manuscript is easy to follow.

Weakness:
1. The channel-wise normalization [a] and k-nearest neighbor clustering [b] are proposed many years ago. Both of them are widely used in the computer vision field. Therefore, the novelty of the paper is limited.
2. The authors should provide evidence to support the claim that DA operations increase the quantization noise of images.
3. The authors should compare with more latest works in the experiment, such as [c][d]. In fact, [d] achieves better performance than the proposed approach in the CUB dataset.
4. The ablation experiments should study why the normalization and geometric average operations contribute to performance improvement.

[a] Dcan: Dual channel-wise alignment networks for unsupervised scene adaptation, CVPR 2018.
[b] In defense of nearest-neighbor based image classification, CVPR 2008.
[c] PaCL: Part-level Contrastive Learning for Fine-grained Few-shot Image Classification, ACM MM 2022.
[d] Few-Shot Classification with Feature Map Reconstruction Networks, CVPR 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed approach is well is clearly explained in the paper. The writing is fluent and easy to understand. However, the idea of the paper lacks originality.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The idea of the paper lacks novelty. The contribution is incremental. Therefore, I believe that this paper should be rejected.

======================================================================================================

Thank the authors for addressing my concerns. After reading the authors’ responses and peer reviews, I decided to keep my score of 3. My main concern is the novelty. The authors claim that they propose a novel feature acquisition network (RFANet) to address the feature acquisition bias of current FSFGIC models. However, the authors also say that the normalization and k-nearest neighbor are not their contributions, which is the main approach written in section 3. Therefore, I believe that the novelty of this paper is limited.

content.title: Revisiting Feature Acquisition Bias for Few-Shot Fine-Grained Image Classification
content.abstract: Recent work on metric-learning based few-shot fine-grained image classification (FSFGIC) has achieved promising success in classification accuracy, where various convolution neural networks with different similarity measures are utilized to learn a common feature representation for each category for FSFGIC. In this paper, we identify and analyze for the first time a fundamental problem of existing metric-learning based FSFGIC methods which fail to effectively address the bias in features obtained from each input image that causes misclassification. To solve this problem, we present a robust feature acquisition network (RFANet) that has the ability to effectively address the bias in the feature information obtained from each input image and guide convolution-based embedding models to significantly increase the accuracy. Our proposed architecture can be easily embedded into any episodic training mechanisms for end-to-end training from scratch. Extensive experiments on FSFGIC tasks demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over the state-of-the-arts.
